Karrie Leduc-Santoro, 11, of Naugatuck has been chosen as a state finalist in the National American Miss Connecticut Pageant to be held July 18-20 at Sturbridge Host Hotel in Sturbridge, Mass. The National American Miss pageants are held for girls ages 4 to18 and have five different age divisions. Leduc-Santoro will be participating in the Miss Connecticut Pre-teen age division, 10 to 12 years old. Leduc-Santoro’s activities include Peer helpers, Homework helpers, chorus, and cartooning club. She enjoys spending time with her family and friends. She takes care of our two dogs and two cats with her little sister. The winner of the pageant will receive a $1,000 cash award, the official crown and banner, a bouquet of roses, and air transportation to compete in the National Pageant in California. All activities and competitions are kept age appropriate. Girls under the age of 12 are not allowed to wear make-up, and there is no swimsuit completion. -CONTRIBUTED

Thoroughbred trainers rarely win races at a 20 percent clip for an entire year. Tom Amoss does so religiously.&nbsp;His 26.4 percent success rate in 2007 marked his 15th consecutive year over 20 percent and his eighth straight over 24.0, upping his career winning percentage to a sensational 23.9.&nbsp;&nbsp;“The greatest thing I can say about our stable is that we are out to win, period.” Amoss said.  The 46-year-old New Orleans native, who races primarily at Fair Grounds and Churchill Downs, finished 15th in victories (149) and 21st in earnings ($4.5 million) nationally last year without a single star in his stable. Of the 110 horses on the 2007 Eclipse Awards ballot, none were trained by Amoss.&nbsp;He didn’t let that deter him from another outstanding year. He wins bunches of races by placing his horses with precision and playing the claiming game with wisdom belying his relative young age.&nbsp; “He’s always been very determined,” his life-long friend, trainer Albert Stall, said. “He was like that as a middle-schooler. He always knew what he wanted, and he went at it full speed.” &nbsp;He still does. That’s why Amoss takes care of himself as well as his horses. He works out four times a week. “For peace of mind,” he said. “I run for half an hour and do weights for 40 minutes. I got very serious about it in 1995.” Asked if he does it because he’s in a stressful business, Amoss replied, “It’s stressful a lot. This profession gives you a lot of variables you can’t control.”&nbsp;So he tries to control the ones he can, and there aren’t too many trainers who do it better. Or who have ever done it better. He is 79th in career victories (1,945), and of the 78 trainers ahead of him, just one, Noble Threewitt, had less starts than Amoss’s 8,143. “That’s good company,” Amoss said. “You better believe I’ll take that.”  When confronted with adversity, Amoss handles that, too. Ask him about the house his family lost to Hurricane Katrina in 2005, and he replies, “It was difficult losing a home in New Orleans, but we didn’t go through anything like what other people went through. My wife and I consider ourselves lucky. Very lucky. We had a place to go.”&nbsp; That was to their other house in Louisville, Kentucky. Now their New Orleans house has been rebuilt. But always, always, it seems that Amoss has had a place to go: the racetrack. &nbsp;“At a young age, I knew I wanted to do this,” he said. “Since I was a kid, I owned horses growing up, Quarter Horses and pleasure horses.”&nbsp;But his parents would never have let him pursue a life with horses without getting a college degree first. “They were insistent that no matter what choice I made, I go to college,” he said. His dad, Jim, was the CEO of a steamship company in New Orleans. His mom, Bertha, is an illustrator of children’s books and the author of a novel, The Chalk Cross. Tom was the second youngest of six boys, all of whom graduated college. The oldest, Dale, became a Rhodes Scholar (after graduating from Yale). The next two oldest also attended Yale. The fourth oldest went to Duke. Tom graduated with a degree in accounting from Louisiana State University, where his roommate was Al Stall. Tom’s younger brother attended Williams College in Massachusetts.   “I had a great childhood,” Amoss said. “I fell in love with horses when I was about 11 or 12.” When he was 13, Stall, whose dad was the head of the Louisiana racing commissioner, took Amoss to the track for the first time. That’s when Amoss had his first look at the backstretch. “When I went back there and saw all that it takes to get these horses raced, it was amazing,” Amoss said. “I was totally infatuated with it. I couldn’t get enough of it. I knew. I knew I was going to train horses. In everything that I did, I was fully aware I was going to train. My parents were comfortable with what I wanted to do. They were very comfortable.” They probably wouldn’t have been comfortable learning that their boy was sneaking a copy of the Daily Racing Form into school every day, or sneaking out of school to go see a race at Fair Grounds. “Never got caught doing that,” Amoss said, a trace of pride still evident 30 years later.Amoss, though, said he got his thrill from the Form not by gambling, but by handicapping. “I was fluent reading the Form,” he said. “For me, it started back then as a real adventure. There’s something about trying to analyze a race and being correct. It wasn’t about cashing a bet. It was about analyzing a race and being correct. They sold the Racing Form at a newsstand. I bought it that day after school. I’d handicap. Racing had a place back then in New Orleans and the race results were on TV. I was able to see how I did that day.”   In high school, Amoss began walking hots for Hall of Famer Jack Van Berg, whose 6,378 victories are second only to the late Dale Baird.&nbsp;Amoss continued walking horses while in college at LSU, first for Van Berg and then for Frankie Brothers. One afternoon, Amoss made quite an impression on one of his professors. “When I was a freshman, I saw my English professor at the track,” Amoss said. “I told him that we (Van Berg) were running a horse that day. I gave it to him and another horse. Both horses won. One paid $70. When I came back to spring semester, English was my best course.”Amoss, though, was more interested in race courses, though he remains a fervent supporter of LSU football, which means he is still smiling after the Tigers blasted Ohio State University to win its second national championship in five years in early January. “I was at the game,” Amoss said the next day. “I’d say outside of horses, it’s one of my excesses,” he said. “I usually make five games a year.”   While in college, Amoss began working for Brothers. “The lesson I learned (from Van Berg and Brothers) was you have to be there,” Amoss said. “It’s hands on. It’s the little things you do around the barn. You work seven days a week. Everybody does.”   Amoss interrupted his training apprenticeship in 1984 to work as a veterinary assistant for Backstretch Surgery, one of the largest practices in Louisiana, run by Dr. Tom David and Dr. Gary Norwood. “They knew what I wanted to do and they went out of their way to show me things,” Amoss said. “That year was probably the most important in my learning process. I wanted to do that. When we had horses with problems, complex things, I learned a lot about legs and which injuries you can continue on with. That was a big year in my learning curve. The whole time I kept a journal.”   After a year, Amoss returned to training as an assistant for Larry Robideaux. “I learned a lot about treating the horses as individuals, not using the same formula to get a horse ready to run,” Amoss said. “He did a very good job of individualizing.”   Amoss spent one year in New York working for trainer John Parisella before opening his own stable in 1987. He was 25. He saddled his first winner, Prize Dream, at Sportsman’s Park in Chicago and won two other races that year from a total of 15 starts. That’s 20 percent, the benchmark of his career. He’s only dipped below that percentage three times in 21 years, in 1989 (19.0), 1990 (17.8) and 1992 (17.1). The average for all trainers is 16 percent. He cites two reasons for his consistent success: keeping his stable to a manageable size and having a group of dedicated workers that have stayed with him for years. “We try to operate with the same size, right about 50 horses, sometimes a little bit bigger,” Amoss said. “One time we had 80 and our win percentage dropped dramatically. We’re very hands on. When you get that big a number, you can’t do everything you want.”   Amoss feels blessed that he has kept a successful team of employees together for years. “I have a very good group who works with me,” he said. “My head assistant is Frank Bernis, and we’ve been together since Day 1. When I was an assistant with John Parisella, he was one of the grooms who worked with me. He’s not unique. I’ve got guys who have been with me for 15 years. You see the same faces year in and year out. We do it together. We all have our input. I’m not so smart that I think I know it all.” Amoss jump-started his career in 1988 with only three horses in his barn. One of them was Fire the Shot, a $16,000 purchase spread among eight partners (including Al Stall). “The other two horses were owned by a volatile guy,” Amoss said. “It was scary.”   Though Fire the Shot had only broken his maiden as a three-year-old, Amoss entered him the 1988 $50,000 Gator Handicap at Louisiana Downs against older horses, one of them Amoss’ other horse. Fire the Shot won the stakes. “I knew the horse wanted to go long,” Amoss said. “A lot of the credit goes to Al.”&nbsp; Amoss’ only other owner removed both of his horses from Amoss, but Fire the Shot’s success caught the attention of John Franks, perennially one of the leading owners in the country. “That was a tremendous break,” Amoss said. “I was his No. 1 guy for four or five years. That made a big difference.”   So has Amoss’ success. Amoss was inducted into the Fair Grounds Hall of Fame in 1999. He was 37. That was the same year he inherited Jack Garey’s Heritage of Gold. You don’t often pick up a horse with a five-race winning streak capped by a 4 ¼-length romp in a Grade 2 Stakes, but in July, 1999, Garey decided to take Heritage of Gold out of Steve Asmussen’s barn and place her in Amoss’ care. “I had trained for Mr. Garey, but she was trained by Steve Asmussen,” Amoss said. “He made a decision to move her. I don’t know why. She was already on her way on what Steve did. She had just won a Grade 2, the Molly Pitcher (at Monmouth Park). She was great. I was lucky to have her. She was a window into a part of the racing scene I didn’t know. She was great, and I got to ride her coattails.”   Heritage of Gold lost three of her first four starts for Amoss, but all were in Grade 1 stakes. She was third in the Go for Wand, fourth in the Flower Bowl on grass, and third, beaten just two lengths by Beautiful Pleasure, in the 1999 Breeders’ Cup Distaff. Her victory was in the Grade 2 Diana Handicap on turf at Saratoga. &nbsp;Amoss gave her time off, and when she returned at the age of five in 2000, she ripped off five consecutive victories in the Grade 3 Oaklawn Breeders’ Cup, the Grade 1 Apple Blossom Handicap, the Grade 2 Louisville Breeders’ Cup, the Grade 3 Fleur de Lis and, on a sloppy track at Saratoga, the Grade 1 Go for Wand. She was odds-on to be champion handicap mare, but she lost her final three starts in 2000, all Grade 1 stakes. She ran third in the Personal Ensign, fourth in the Spinster and third by three lengths to Spain in the Breeders’ Cup Distaff. “She was so easy to train,” Amoss said. “She never ever had an unsound day.” Amoss’ success has continued this decade, even as he culled a second career as a TV analyst, first with ESPN, then with the Television Games Network (TVG). “I got a chance to do a piece on ESPN in the mid-90’s, a half hour show for them that was an absolute disaster,” Amoss said. “That was the end of my ESPN career. But I was friends of someone who worked for TVG. They asked me to be a one-time analyst. I was nervous, very nervous. Very unprepared. It was awful. The first show I did was bad, but slowly but surely I got to where I was comfortable in front of the camera. I still work for TVG. I really enjoy it.” On the track in 2004, he posted his best winning percentage (28.9). Much of his success has come with claimers. “I try to put myself in the owner’s shoes and try to cut losses as quickly as possible,” he said. “It’s a much better solution to the problem.”   There was no solution when Hurricane Katrina battered New Orleans in the late summer of 2005. Amoss and his wife Colleen, who met at LSU, had just registered their two girls, Ashley and Haley, in high school in New Orleans, rather than in Louisville, Kentucky. “They hadn’t been in school for more than a week and a half,” Amoss said. “Two days after the storm, when it became apparent the city wasn’t going to survive, we were lucky. We were able to put the kids back (in school) in Louisville. Don‘t make my case a tragedy.” Still, when he and his wife returned to New Orleans, they had to deal with a painful reality. “The first time we came back was a month after the storm,” Amoss said. “The water had subsided. They let us back for an hour. We had eight feet of water in the house. The entire neighborhood was covered with gray soot. It was like being in a black and white movie. No colors. Our little guppy, he survived. So we brought him back to Louisville.&nbsp; “Everything that we had in the house was lost: clothes, appliances. We lost it all. But all you had to do was look at people who didn’t have a place to go. In my neighborhood, I had the only house that was built back.”   Asked about his greatest thrill in racing since Heritage of Gold, Amoss mentioned two horses. The first had been third in a non-winners of two at Churchill Downs. “He won an allowance race on grass going 5 ½ furlongs,” Amoss said. “It was a surface he hadn’t run on before, and at a distance he wasn’t used to. We definitely made a difference. I get great satisfaction when the barn made a difference.”  Then Amoss mentioned Hot Wells. “I claimed him for $12,500 at Ellis Park,” Amoss said. “He went on to become a graded stakes winner (the 1998 Grade 3 Southwest Stakes) and ran fourth in the (1988) Preakness to Real Quiet. He made a move on the leaders up to second. I said, ‘Gee, he’s got a shot.’ I told my wife afterwards, `If you could bottle that feeling, you could sell it for any price in the world.’” Amoss works very hard to reproduce that feeling. “For someone who’s done it as long as he had, he maintains a high level of energy and intensity,” his buddy Al Stall said. “He gets there very early. He’s on top of his horses.”   That’s because Amoss’ enjoyment of racing is as evident now as it was more than 30 years ago when he visited a racetrack for the first time. “You have to enjoy it,” he said. “It’s a way of life.”For Amoss, it’s a very successful way of life.
